title: India’s Stake in the Global Subsea Cable Race
gist: Charukeshi Bhatt argues India consumes a large share of global internet traffic but barely participates in subsea cable ownership, manufacturing or repair: 18 international cables across 23 landings versus Singapore's 28 cables, with Mumbai alone the gateway for 95 percent of India's international bandwidth and only two maintenance providers (Singapore and Dubai) serving Indian waters. As hyperscaler capital rewrites cable routing economics through projects like the 50,000-kilometre Project Waterworth, she warns India's connectivity map could be redrawn by foreign players and recommends supplementing the underdelivering Quad with Australia, African and Gulf partnerships.

themes.theme: Why subsea cables are strategic for India

insights.claim: Undersea cables transmit nearly 99 percent of global data traffic and offer significantly faster and more reliable transmission than satellites, making them the indispensable foundation of modern digital economies.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Anchors why cable infrastructure, not satellite constellations, is the binding physical constraint on digital and AI economies.
insights.locator: Undersea cables form the largely invisible but indispensable foundation

insights.claim: The global cable network comprises roughly 600 cables stretching approximately 1.5 million kilometers, and the Indian Ocean Region — home to over half the world's internet users and several fast-digitizing economies — is where demand for newer high-capacity systems is most pressing.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Sizes the installed base and locates the demand growth — the IOR is where new cable capex will concentrate.
insights.locator: Strategic Importance of Subsea Cables for India

insights.claim: Countries like India are attracting huge AI infrastructure investment and positioning themselves as serious players in the global AI economy, but all of it rests on robust connectivity immune from sudden disruptions.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Cable resilience is an unpriced dependency in India's AI-datacenter buildout thesis — a physical-layer risk to compute investments.
insights.locator: Fast emerging as a hub for AI use-cases and compute

insights.claim: Cables in the Indian Ocean Region converge at strategic choke points including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea corridor and the Strait of Malacca, creating potential single points of failure where any disruption will likely affect all cable lines in the area.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Maps the specific geographies where a single incident can take out multi-continent connectivity — the correlation risk in digital infrastructure.
insights.locator: The IOR is particularly vulnerable to sudden disruptions

insights.claim: The 2024 disruption of the Asia-Africa-Europe-1 line caused a near-total internet blackout in Ethiopia and over 80 percent connectivity loss in Somalia, demonstrating the concrete consequences of cable chokepoint concentration.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A precedent showing single-cable failure can produce national-scale outages — the downside case for economies without route redundancy.
insights.locator: The 2024 disruption of the Asia-Africa-Europe-1 line

insights.claim: Cables have historically been routed through straits offering the shortest path to limit costs, with seventeen international cables connecting Europe to Africa and Asia passing through the Bab-al-Mandeb strait, but rising instability can convert these straits into geopolitical chokepoints and erode their status as the most economical routes.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Risk of blockade and longer repair timelines is starting to outweigh distance costs — a structural shift in where new cables will be laid.
insights.locator: However, the economic logic governing cable routes is slowly changing

insights.claim: Hyperscaler entry is altering the economics of routes once considered financially unviable, as demonstrated by Project Waterworth stretching over 50,000 kilometers across the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Ocean — longer routes bypassing vulnerable corridors are no longer cost-prohibitive.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Big Tech balance sheets, not telco consortium economics, now set cable routing — a demand tailwind for cable manufacturers and ship operators.
insights.locator: The entry of hyperscalers into global subsea cable infrastructure

insights.claim: If cables are rerouted by foreign hyperscalers, India's connectivity infrastructure could be redrawn during this phase of network expansion without meaningful domestic participation.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A time-limited window: routing decisions being made now will lock in India's position for a cable generation.
insights.locator: For countries like India, the concern is that if these cables

insights.claim: The subsea cable industry splits into four participant types — manufacturers who build and lay cables, telecom carriers who own capacity via consortium arrangements, hyperscalers who have moved from leasing into ownership across the full data infrastructure stack, and repair firms with specialized vessels.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A value-chain map for locating where cable capex accrues and which layer is most exposed to geopolitical contracting decisions.
insights.locator: India’s Current Capabilities

insights.claim: Three firms dominate cable manufacturing — Alcatel Submarine Networks of France, SubCom of the United States and NEC of Japan — and because manufacturing capacity is so geographically concentrated, states are taking direct interest in these firms and contracting decisions are becoming geopolitical.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A three-supplier bottleneck in a growth market — pricing power and political scrutiny both concentrate in ASN, SubCom and NEC.
insights.locator: Three key players dominate the cable manufacturing market

insights.claim: India grew from seventeen international subsea cables at around fourteen landing stations in 2024 to eighteen cables across twenty-three distinct landings by 2025, while Singapore — geographically smaller than Mumbai — currently has twenty-eight cables across eight landing stations.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A stark like-for-like benchmark showing India's cable footprint is subscale relative to its data economy — the gap that new investment must close.
insights.locator: India’s current footprint in the global subsea cable network is limited

insights.claim: The Mumbai coastline alone acts as the gateway for ninety-five percent of India's international bandwidth, with landing stations concentrated across just five cities — Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi, Tuticorin and Thiruvananthapuram.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Extreme single-point concentration in Mumbai is India's largest digital infrastructure vulnerability and the argument for east-coast landings.
insights.locator: For India, the Mumbai coastline alone acts as the gateway

insights.claim: Newer cable systems landing along India's eastern coast will help reduce congestion at the Mumbai site, with domestic participation limited to a small set of established telecom firms including Tata Communications, Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio, Sify Technologies and BSNL.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Names the narrow set of Indian companies positioned to capture any policy-driven expansion of domestic cable participation.
insights.locator: Newer cables systems are landing along India’s eastern coast

insights.claim: Indian waters are served by only two cable maintenance providers, based in Singapore and Dubai, with the nearest cable depot for spare cables located in Galle, Sri Lanka.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Repair dependency means Indian outage duration is set by foreign vessel availability — a concrete gap a domestic repair capability could fill.
insights.locator: Even in cable repair, there are dependencies

insights.claim: The Quad's engagement with subsea cables has been shaped by shared concerns over China's expanding role in the Indo-Pacific cable ecosystem in both market share and emerging capabilities, producing the 2023 Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience, the 2024 New York Principles, a resilience center in Australia, and the US-Japan-Australia-backed Micronesia-Kiribati-Nauru cable that made final landing in 2025.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Inventories what Quad cable cooperation has actually delivered, which is the baseline for judging whether more is coming.
insights.locator: Assessing the Quad

insights.claim: Tangible progress on subsea cables has come through bilateral or trilateral arrangements rather than Quad-wide mechanisms, and India was not among the first endorsers of the 2024 New York Principles that every other Quad member endorsed.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Discounts the Quad as an execution vehicle for cable investment — bilateral deals are where commitments actually land.
insights.locator: However, much of the tangible progress can be seen in bilateral

insights.claim: Cable repair cooperation across the Quad's dispersed geography is inherently constrained because repairs are time-sensitive but distance-bound — even Singapore dispatching repair ships for faults near India means response times running into days.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Physics defeats the diplomacy: repair capability must be regional, which argues for local depots and vessels over multilateral frameworks.
insights.locator: Firstly, while all four members situate subsea infrastructure

insights.claim: Quad members' capabilities are deeply uneven — the US and Japan host dominant players SubCom and NEC accounting for a substantial share of global cable-laying and maintenance, Australia has a model regulatory and financing framework with direct Pacific investment, while India remains a relatively limited participant.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Capability asymmetry explains why cooperation defaults to bilateral pairings and what each partner brings that India can source.
insights.locator: Secondly, and more fundamentally, the unevenness in the capabilities

insights.claim: Just as cable systems require redundancy, so do cooperation mechanisms — India should keep existing partnerships while adding alternatives bound by complementary geography and shared regional connectivity stakes rather than shared interest alone.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: A diversification principle applied to diplomacy — signals India will pursue multiple overlapping cable partnerships rather than one bloc.
insights.quote: Cable systems require redundancy. So too will cooperation mechanisms.
insights.locator: What Should India Do?

insights.claim: Australia is a strong candidate partner because it brings financing and regulatory experience plus a Pacific cable role, and the Australia-India Cyber and Critical Technology Partnership already serves as a ready anchor for deeper technical and regulatory engagement.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
entities: Australia-India Cyber and Critical Technology Partnership
insights.so_what: Names the specific existing bilateral instrument through which India-Australia cable cooperation would most plausibly be operationalized.
insights.locator: A potential candidate could be Australia

insights.claim: African countries are valuable potential cable partners for India because both regions see rapid growth in data demand and AI infrastructure, and a routing corridor through the Indian Ocean could support co-investment in shared infrastructure serving both sides.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Identifies an India-Africa cable corridor as a co-investment opportunity that would also diversify away from Red Sea chokepoints.
insights.locator: African countries could also be valuable partners

insights.claim: Oman and Saudi Arabia are actively investing in digital infrastructure and positioning themselves as hubs linking Asia, Africa and Europe, making them important potential cable partners for India.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Gulf digital-hub ambitions create a competing set of landing points India could either partner with or be bypassed by.
insights.locator: In West Asia, both Oman and Saudi Arabia

insights.claim: As the financial logic determining cable deployment and routing undergoes gradual change, India has a window to influence how this infrastructure develops in its own region — a window tied to the current expansion phase rather than open-ended.
insights.speaker: Charukeshi Bhatt
insights.so_what: Frames Indian cable policy as time-sensitive, implying near-term regulatory or financing moves rather than gradual drift.
insights.quote: India must use this window to influence how this infrastructure develops in its own region
insights.locator: Subsea cables will only continue to amass more strategic importance
